clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive low-GGT cholestasis caused by ABCB11 mutations encoding BSEP, the principal canalicular bile salt export pump; because expression is essentially liver-restricted, there are no extrahepatic features, in contrast with PFIC1.
Onset is typically neonatal and progression is more rapid than PFIC1, often with giant-cell hepatitis on biopsy.
Serum bile acids are markedly elevated with a disproportionately low GGT, and alpha-fetoprotein may be raised.
There is a substantial risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma in early childhood, so tumour surveillance with imaging and alpha-fetoprotein monitoring is essential.
Vitamin K-dependent coagulopathy and bleeding can be the presenting feature before jaundice is recognised.
Absent or reduced canalicular BSEP on immunohistochemistry supports the diagnosis, though some missense variants retain partial function and milder phenotypes.
Allelic disorders include the milder episodic benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 (BRIC2) and a contribution to intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy.
After transplantation, alloimmune disease from anti-BSEP antibodies can produce a cholestatic picture mimicking disease recurrence in the graft.
reference.pathophysiology: ABCB11 encodes BSEP, an ATP-binding cassette transporter that is the rate-limiting canalicular pump for secretion of monovalent bile salts into bile. Loss of function prevents export of bile acids, so they accumulate within hepatocytes, producing cholestatic injury, giant-cell transformation and progressive fibrosis; the severe reduction in biliary bile acids also impairs micelle formation and fat absorption. Because BSEP is expressed almost exclusively in hepatocytes, the disease is confined to the liver, distinguishing it from PFIC1. The sustained intracellular exposure to cytotoxic bile acids underlies a markedly increased risk of malignant transformation to hepatocellular carcinoma and cholangiocarcinoma even in infancy, with genotype broadly correlating with severity, residual transporter function and cancer risk.
additionalDifferentials: PFIC type 1 (ATP8B1/FIC1 deficiency) — low GGT with extrahepatic diarrhoea and deafness
Inborn errors of bile acid synthesis
additionalInvestigations: Serum total bile acids with paired serum GGT (low or normal)
Serum alpha-fetoprotein for baseline and surveillance
Liver biopsy with BSEP immunostaining and assessment for giant-cell hepatitis
Liver ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging for tumour surveillance
Coagulation profile and fat-soluble vitamin levels
redFlags: Coagulopathy or bleeding at presentation from vitamin K deficiency
Rising alpha-fetoprotein or a focal liver lesion suggesting malignancy
Rapid progression to cirrhosis within the first years of life
Hepatic decompensation with ascites or variceal bleeding
reference.prognosis: Disease often progresses rapidly to cirrhosis within the first years of life and carries a high childhood risk of hepatobiliary malignancy. Biliary diversion helps some children and transplantation is usually curative for the liver disease, but antibody-mediated recurrence can occur.
pitfalls: Reading a low or normal GGT as reassuring against severe cholestasis
Failing to institute malignancy surveillance despite young age
Missing a bleeding tendency that reflects fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Assuming transplantation removes all risk while overlooking alloimmune BSEP recurrence
references: Clinical genetics of liver disease references
management: Ileal bile acid transporter inhibitors such as odevixibat or maralixibat to interrupt bile acid recycling and reduce pruritus and hepatocellular bile acid injury
Antipruritic therapy with rifampicin and bile acid sequestrants, with ursodeoxycholic acid as an adjunct
Fat-soluble vitamin supplementation including vitamin K to correct coagulopathy, plus medium-chain-triglyceride nutritional support
Surgical biliary diversion for symptom control and disease modification in suitable children
Intensive hepatobiliary malignancy surveillance from early childhood with alpha-fetoprotein and liver ultrasound and cross-sectional imaging
Liver transplantation for end-stage disease or malignancy, with awareness of antibody-mediated BSEP recurrence in the graft
Genetic counselling and cascade family testing for this autosomal recessive ABCB11 disorder
